checks.claim: Key: the nucleus is made of protons and neutrons
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a central nucleus composed of positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons'.

checks.claim: Stem: a gold nucleus is less than a ten-thousandth as wide as the whole atom
checks.note: Gold atomic radius 144 pm (Grokipedia, Gold); Au-197 rms charge radius 5.44 fm (NUMOR), about 7 fm by r0*A^(1/3). Ratio about 1/20,000 to 1/26,000, so 'less than a ten-thousandth' holds. Grokipedia Rutherford model: nuclear radius 'less than 1/10,000 that of the atom'.

checks.claim: Wrong: protons and electrons
checks.note: The pre-1932 'nuclear electrons' belief, now known false; the stem asks what the nucleus IS made of, and the context says so.

checks.claim: Wrong: neutrons and electrons; protons, neutrons and electrons
checks.note: Electrons are in the cloud outside the nucleus.

checks.claim: Context: gold nucleus 79 protons and 118 neutrons; 79 electrons
checks.note: Grokipedia: Au-197 'comprises 79 protons and 118 neutrons'; atomic number 79; gold's only stable isotope.

checks.claim: Context: electron about 1/1836 of a proton's mass
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'approximately 1/1836 that of a proton'.

checks.claim: Context: nucleus holds over 99.9 percent of the atom's mass
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the nucleus holds over 99.9% of the atom's mass'.

checks.claim: Context: until the neutron was found in 1932, physicists thought a nucleus was protons and electrons
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'physicists assumed that the atomic nucleus was composed of protons and nuclear electrons'.

checks.claim: Lead's atomic number is 82; gold's is 79
Alchemists spent centuries trying to turn lead into gold
checks.note: Chrysopoeia from Greco-Roman Egypt (1st c. BCE) into the 18th century; lead the classic base metal.

checks.claim: Key: losing three protons from its nucleus would make lead into gold
checks.note: Z 'uniquely identifies the chemical element'. CERN ALICE (2025): 'To create gold (a nucleus containing 79 protons), three protons must be removed from a lead nucleus', and they observed it happen.

checks.claim: Wrong: losing three neutrons
checks.note: Still lead, another isotope.

checks.claim: Wrong: losing three electrons / gaining three electrons
checks.note: Still lead, an ion: the protons are unchanged.

checks.claim: Context: chemistry moves electrons and never touches the nucleus; no alchemist's furnace could make gold
checks.note: Chrysopoeia was 'never achieved through chemical means'; chemical reactions leave nuclei unchanged. Gold has been made only by nuclear means (Seaborg 1980 from bismuth; CERN from lead), in traces.

checks.claim: Stem: a helium atom has 2 protons, 2 neutrons, 2 electrons and no net charge
checks.note: True of helium-4, nearly all natural helium (helium-3 has one neutron); fine at this level.

checks.claim: Stem: alpha particles, the kind Geiger and Marsden fired at gold foil, are helium atoms stripped of both electrons
checks.note: 'identical to the nucleus of a helium-4 atom'; Rutherford and Royds (1909) showed they are doubly ionised helium; used in the Geiger-Marsden foil work.

checks.claim: Key: a positive charge of two
checks.note: 'a positive charge of +2 elementary charges due to the two protons'.

checks.claim: Wrong: plus four; minus two; no charge
checks.note: Neutrons carry no charge, so not +4; no electrons left, so not negative or neutral.

checks.claim: Context: in a neutral atom electrons cancel the protons' charge exactly
Stem: sodium and potassium are soft, silvery metals that react strongly with water
checks.note: Sodium 'soft, bright, silvery-white', 'vigorous exothermic reaction' with water; potassium soft, silvery-white, 'reacts violently with water'.

checks.claim: Stem: sodium has 11 electrons, potassium 19
checks.note: Atomic numbers 11 and 19 (neutral atoms).

checks.claim: Key: the same number of outer electrons
checks.note: Valence electrons 'determine an element's reactivity and chemical properties'; Group 1 metals 'each have one valence electron, making them highly reactive'.

checks.claim: Wrong: same number of inner electrons
checks.note: [Ne]3s1 has 10 inner electrons; [Ar]4s1 has 18.

checks.claim: Wrong: same number of electron shells
checks.note: Valence electron in shell 3 (3s) for sodium, shell 4 (4s) for potassium.

checks.claim: Wrong: same number of particles in the nucleus
checks.note: Sodium-23 (only stable isotope) vs potassium-39 (93.26 percent of potassium).

checks.claim: Context: shells 2,8,1 and 2,8,8,1; one easily lost valence electron; 10 vs 18 inner, 3 vs 4 shells, nuclei of 23 and 39 particles
checks.note: The 39 is potassium-39, the dominant isotope; fine at this level.

checks.claim: Stem: Thomson, cathode rays, a glass tube pumped almost empty, Cambridge, 1897
checks.note: The paper is dated 'Cambridge, Aug. 7, 1897' (Cavendish Laboratory).

checks.claim: Stem: the beam bent toward the positive plate, and a magnet bent it too
checks.note: Thomson: deflected 'as if they were negatively electrified'; 'the rays were depressed when the upper plate was connected with the negative pole'; also bent by a magnet. Grokipedia: 'deflected toward the positively charged plate'.

checks.claim: Key: Thomson concluded the rays were negatively charged pieces of atoms
checks.note: He proposed the gas molecules are 'dissociated and are split up' into corpuscles, 'the substance from which all the chemical elements are built up'.

checks.claim: Wrong: negatively charged atoms of the gas
checks.note: The Crookes/Schuster view (charged atoms); Thomson's m/e, the same for every gas and far below the hydrogen ion's, ruled it out.

checks.claim: Wrong: negatively charged atoms of the metal
checks.note: m/e 'came out the same whatever the material of the electrode'.

checks.claim: Wrong: waves in the ether, like waves of light
checks.note: The German view (Hertz, Goldstein, Wiedemann); Thomson showed charged-particle bending.

checks.claim: Context: the two bends gave mass per unit charge, the same whatever gas and cathode metal
checks.note: 'the value of m/e is independent of the nature of the gas'; 'came out the same whatever the material of the electrode'.

checks.claim: Context: 'It [the figure] showed the particles were far lighter than a hydrogen atom'
checks.note: The m/e figure alone could not show this, and Thomson said so in the same 1897 paper: 'The smallness of m/e may be due to the smallness of m or the largeness of e, or to a combination of these two.' He argued the carriers were 'small compared with ordinary molecules' from Lenard's absorption results, and the small mass was settled once he measured the charge in 1899 (Wikipedia: m/e 'over a thousand times lower than that of a hydrogen ion', 'suggesting either that the particles were very light and/or very highly charged'). Textbooks often simplify it this way, so not a hard error, but it misstates what 1897 showed. Fix: 'Their mass for each unit of charge was about a thousandth of a hydrogen ion's, which pointed to particles far lighter than a hydrogen atom; his measurement of their charge in 1899 bore it out (about 1,800 times lighter, by today's measure).'

checks.claim: Context: hydrogen the lightest atom; electron about 1,800 times lighter by today's measure
checks.note: Hydrogen atom to electron mass ratio about 1837.

checks.claim: Context: he called them corpuscles; now called electrons
checks.note: 'which he termed corpuscles'; 'the name electron was later adopted'.

checks.claim: Stem: Thomson's model of 1904 balanced the electrons with an equal positive charge
Key: the positive charge spread evenly all through the atom
checks.note: Thomson 1904: corpuscles 'moving about in a sphere of uniform positive electrification'.

checks.claim: Wrong: packed into one tiny, heavy centre
checks.note: Rutherford's 1911 picture.

checks.claim: Wrong: held in a thin shell around the outside
Wrong: carried by a few large positive particles
checks.note: Wrong for 1904 (a continuous uniform sphere). In 1910 Thomson modelled the positive charge as many small units, each equal to an electron's charge, spread evenly: still not 'a few large' ones, and the stem names 1904.

checks.claim: Context: later nicknamed the plum pudding; Thomson never used the name
checks.note: Wikipedia: the analogy 'was never used by Thomson nor his colleagues'; first known in 1906 in The Chemist and Druggist.

checks.claim: Context: the model predicted alphas through gold foil would bend a few degrees at most
checks.note: Grokipedia: total deflections 'up to about 2 degrees', 'only a few degrees at most'. (The figure was worked out from Thomson's model, largely by Rutherford; 'his model predicted' is fair.)

checks.claim: Context: the tiny, heavy centre came later, from Rutherford
Stem: Geiger and his undergraduate student Marsden, Rutherford's laboratory at Manchester, 1909
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'a physics undergraduate student studying under Geiger'; AIP: 'a 19-year-old student in Honours Physics'; the back-scattering paper ('On a Diffuse Reflection of the a-Particles') was submitted May 1909. Gold was among the foils tested (with platinum, lead and others).

checks.claim: Stem: in a darkened room they counted the faint flash each particle made on a screen
checks.note: Zinc sulfide scintillations counted through a microscope 'in a darkened observation room'.

checks.claim: Stem: a very few bounced back toward their source
checks.note: About 1 in 8,000 reflected (thick platinum, 1909).

checks.claim: Stem: Rutherford worked it out in 1911
checks.note: Abstract read 7 March 1911; full paper in the Philosophical Magazine, May 1911.

checks.claim: Key: each atom has a tiny, heavy centre
checks.note: AIP: most of the mass and charge concentrated in 'a very small central body'.

checks.claim: Wrong: electrons hard and heavy; charge spread out evenly; packed solid all through
checks.note: Electrons are too light to turn an alpha back; even spread is Thomson's model, which the bounces refuted; a solid atom contradicts most particles passing through.

checks.claim: Context: 'now called the nucleus'
checks.note: AIP: in 1911 he spoke of a 'charged center', not yet 'nucleus' (Wikipedia: the term from 1912). The context's wording avoids the dispute.

checks.claim: Context: atoms packed solid would have turned back far more than a few
checks.note: Reasoning, fair at this level: a foil a thousand or more solid atoms deep would stop or turn back nearly every particle.

checks.claim: Context: Rutherford later likened it to a 15-inch shell fired at tissue paper coming back to hit him (paraphrase, not quoted)
checks.note: Lecture at Cambridge, 15 October 1936, printed in his 1938 book (AIP cites p. 68).

checks.claim: Stem: the foil was very thin but many atoms thick
checks.note: Grokipedia: about 400 nm, 'or 1000 atomic layers for gold'; Wikipedia: 1.5 micrometres would be about 10,000 atoms thick.

checks.claim: Stem: almost every alpha went straight through or bent only slightly
checks.note: 'the vast majority of alpha particles passed through thin metal foils' with minimal deflection.

checks.claim: Key: most of each atom is empty space
checks.note: OpenStax: the particles 'must have traveled through essentially empty space inside the atom'; Grokipedia: 'implying that atoms are mostly empty space'. Historical nuance only: Thomson's diffuse model also expected most alphas to pass through, so the conclusion leans on the rare bounces too (the context does tie it to the tiny nucleus). Optional tightening of the stem: 'Together with the rare few that bounced back, what did that show?'

checks.claim: Wrong: alpha particles carry no electric charge
checks.note: They carry +2.

checks.claim: Wrong: alpha particles are lighter than electrons
checks.note: About 7,300 times an electron's mass.

checks.claim: Wrong: the foil had gaps between its atoms
checks.note: Ruled out by the stem: with a thousand or more atomic layers no straight path avoids every atom.

checks.claim: Context: missed the tiny nucleus, met only electrons, far too light to turn it
checks.note: 'their combined mass is low, they have a negligible effect on the alpha particle'.

checks.claim: Context: nucleus less than a ten-thousandth of the atom's width
checks.note: 'the radius of the nucleus being less than 1/10,000 that of the atom'.

checks.claim: Context: alpha charge plus two; about 7,300 times an electron's mass
checks.note: 'approximately 7300 times that of an electron' (6.644e-27 kg / 9.109e-31 kg = 7,294).

checks.claim: Stem: Bohr came to Manchester in 1912 to work with Rutherford
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'relocated to the Victoria University of Manchester in early 1912 to collaborate with Ernest Rutherford' (March to July 1912), after Thomson's laboratory at Cambridge from September 1911.

checks.claim: Stem: hydrogen gas carrying a current glows in a few sharp colours, not a smooth rainbow
checks.note: Four visible lines: red 656.3 nm, cyan 486.1 nm, blue 434.0 nm, violet 410.2 nm.

checks.claim: Stem: Bohr explained it in 1913
checks.note: His 1913 papers explained the hydrogen lines by jumps between stationary states.

checks.claim: Key: electrons can only be at certain energy levels
checks.note: Stationary states with discrete energies; light emitted on a transition, its energy equal to the difference.

checks.claim: Wrong: they spiral steadily in toward the nucleus
checks.note: That is the classical prediction Bohr's rule forbade ('an inward spiral into the nucleus within about 10^-8 seconds').

checks.claim: Wrong: they can circle at any distance at all
checks.note: Classical physics; Bohr allowed only set orbits.

checks.claim: Wrong: they stay fixed in place round the nucleus
checks.note: Meant as 'motionless', which is wrong (Bohr's electrons orbit). But 'fixed' is the very word many sources and classrooms use for Bohr's model: Grokipedia Atom, 'electrons orbiting in fixed energy levels'; Grokipedia Balmer series, 'fixed energy levels'; textbooks, 'fixed orbits'; and Bohr called them 'stationary states'. A pupil taught 'fixed orbits' can defend this choice. Fix: 'They sit still, never moving, beside the nucleus' (or 'They never move from one spot').

checks.claim: Context: an electron keeps to 'one of a few set energy levels'
checks.note: Bohr's levels run n = 1, 2, 3, ... without end (E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV); there are not 'a few'. Fix: 'keeps to one of its set energy levels'.

checks.claim: Context: gives off light only when it drops to a lower level; each drop a set size, so one set colour
checks.note: Photon energy equals the level difference (some drops give ultraviolet or infrared rather than a visible colour; acceptable).

checks.claim: Context: by older physics an electron could circle at any distance and would spiral into the nucleus
Context: later physicists replaced the orbits with a probability cloud but kept the energy levels
checks.note: Wave mechanics 'superseded the Bohr model's classical orbits'; its solution 'exactly matched Bohr's formula' for hydrogen's levels; electrons 'occupy probabilistic orbitals'.

checks.claim: Stem: beryllium struck by alpha particles gives off an unusually penetrating radiation
checks.note: Bothe and Becker, 1930: 'an unusually penetrating radiation was produced'.

checks.claim: Stem: aimed at paraffin wax, it knocks protons out at high speed
checks.note: Joliot-Curies, 1932: protons of about 5 to 5.7 MeV ejected from paraffin.

checks.claim: Stem: Chadwick at the Cavendish, Cambridge, 1932, measuring how hard it struck different kinds of atoms
checks.note: Targets included paraffin and gases (helium, nitrogen, oxygen, argon); recoil energies measured; Nature letter dated 27 February 1932.

checks.claim: Key: neutral particles about as heavy as protons
checks.note: 'electrically neutral particles with mass comparable to the proton'; his 1932 estimate 1.005 to 1.008 Da.

checks.claim: Wrong: gamma rays, a kind of light with great energy
checks.note: The Bothe-Becker and Joliot-Curie reading, which Chadwick refuted.

checks.claim: Wrong: fast electrons thrown out of the beryllium; protons thrown out of the beryllium nuclei
checks.note: The radiation was not deflected by an electric field and left no ionisation, so it was not a charged particle.

checks.claim: Context: Irène Joliot-Curie and Frédéric Joliot in Paris took it for gamma rays
checks.note: They 'attributed [it] to exceptionally high-energy gamma rays'; they worked at the Radium Institute in Paris.

checks.claim: Context: light would need impossibly great energy to knock protons out so hard
checks.note: A gamma ray 'would have to have impossibly high energy (50 MeV) to scatter a massive proton'.

checks.claim: Context: no charge, so it left no track and slipped through matter
checks.note: Passes through materials 'without producing ionization tracks'.

checks.claim: Context: Rutherford predicted it in 1920
checks.note: 1920 Bakerian lecture: 'the neutron, a neutral particle of mass 1'.

checks.claim: Context: won Chadwick the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics
checks.note: Sole recipient, 'for the discovery of the neutron'.

unit_notes: No hard errors found. Two uncertain: 944f57c3e1 (context says Thomson's m/e figure alone showed the particles were lighter than hydrogen; Thomson himself said in 1897 that a small m/e could mean small mass or large charge, and the mass was settled with his 1899 charge measurement) and aaa8525a5a (the wrong choice 'They stay fixed in place round the nucleus' collides with the common 'fixed orbits / fixed energy levels' wording for Bohr's model; and the context's 'a few set energy levels' should be 'its set energy levels'). Atomic history checked against Grokipedia, Wikipedia, AIP and Thomson's 1897 paper: Geiger and Marsden's back-scattering 1909, Rutherford's paper 1911 (he said 'charged center', not yet 'nucleus', which the draft handles), Thomson's 1904 uniform sphere, Bohr 1913, Chadwick 1932. Gold nucleus to atom width about 1/20,000 to 1/26,000, so 'less than a ten-thousandth' holds. No figures here change over time.
